heading: **མིག་མ་བྲིས་པས་ཕར་ཕྱིན་གཞན་ཚང་ཡང་རྣམ་མཁྱེན་མི་ཐོབ་པའི་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second is the single verse beginning with "when wisdom." When those other virtuous qualities, such as generosity, are thoroughly grasped by the wisdom that does not conceptualize the three spheres, at that time they find an eye, and having obtained the name of this perfection of wisdom, one attains the ability to proceed easily to the city of omniscience. To illustrate this: if a painting of a human figure or the like is completely drawn in every other respect, but it lacks only the eye—if it is incomplete—then just as one does not receive the reward for the painting because it is not finished due to the eye not being painted, this is the manner in which the fruition is not attained if wisdom is absent, even if other virtues are complete. Thus, one should know that the essence of the Mahāyāna path is to possess non-apprehension in dedication, with a mind of omniscience that is directed toward the mother of fruition—which is not usurped by other paths—by means of an intellect that is certain to ripen solely into the primordial wisdom of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, based on the wisdom that knows the suchness of all phenomena, which transforms all paths into that emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.

The first is the single verse beginning with "the blind and the guide." Just as even if millions of blind people who lack a guide to lead them on the path were to gather together, they would neither see nor know the path lying before them, and thus it is impossible for them to enter that path and proceed to another city—for there is no such possibility—in the same way, if this perfection of wisdom, which is like an eye, is absent, then the five perfections, such as generosity, which are like the blind from their own side, are not grasped by the wisdom that acts as a guide to lead them in that direction. Because they lack that companion, they do not know the noble path, and therefore they are incapable of reaching the city of perfect enlightenment.

heading: **ལམ་ཕར་ཕྱིན་དག་པ་ཐོབ་ཚུལ།**
translation: The second part consists of two points: showing how one enters the ranks of the perfection of wisdom through non-apprehension by way of the analogy of space, and the manner in which the path is not completely purified if one is separated from that.

To illustrate this: if a painting of a human figure or the like is completely drawn in every other respect, but it lacks only the eye—if it is incomplete—then just as one does not receive the reward for the painting because it is not finished due to the eye not being painted, this is the manner in which the fruition is not attained if wisdom is absent, even if other virtues are complete. Thus, one should know that the essence of the Mahāyāna path is to possess non-apprehension in dedication, with a mind of omniscience that is directed toward the mother of fruition—which is not usurped by other paths—by means of an intellect that is certain to ripen solely into the primordial wisdom of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects, based on the wisdom that knows the suchness of all phenomena, which transforms all paths into that emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects.

The first point consists of one verse, "A bodhisattva..." and so forth. Any bodhisattva who, during the time they practiced in previous lifetimes, listened to, grasped, and contemplated the meaning of this profound perfection of wisdom, will, upon being born in this world, become skilled in the meaning of the perfection of wisdom due to the power of those previous causes. Having become free from hesitation regarding it, as soon as they hear this text, that person generates the perception of the Teacher, thinking, "I have seen the Teacher." By the cause of that, they will quickly realize the great peaceful enlightenment.

heading: **དེས་ན་ཡུམ་ལ་དད་པས་བརྩོན་པར་གདམས་པ།**
translation: The third point consists of one verse, "Therefore..." and so forth. Because there are great benefits if one has faith, and great faults if one does not, "Therefore, if you desire to touch the supreme wisdom of the buddhas, you should have faith in this Mother of the Victors." This is the uncommon cause, without which that [wisdom] cannot arise. At this time, when we have met with the teachings of the Tathāgata, which are like an island of precious jewels, we must ensure that there is a result. For example, it would be improper for merchants to go to an island of jewels, only to have their previous trade goods exhausted and, without having gained any new profit in jewels, return empty-handed. Similarly, even if one has the jewel of the profound perfection of wisdom in hand, one should not act in such a way that, by failing to appreciate it and casting it aside, one exhausts one's previous merit through the cause of abandoning the Dharma.

Cultivating in meditative equipoise.

heading: **རྣམ་པར་དག་པའི་ཡེ་ཤེས་ཀྱི་ངོ་བོ།**
translation:
The essence of purified primordial wisdom: The first, the essence, consists of one verse, "The purity of form..." and so forth. Meditating on the single taste of all things as the great, stainless, luminous expanse of reality—the essence of which is primordially pure, naturally beyond sorrow, perfectly awakened, naturally luminous, and primordially unborn and unceasing in its equality—is the essence of the primordial wisdom of meditative equipoise.

What is the manner of this? As indicated by the phrase "the purity of form," all phenomena, from the objects of knowledge such as form up to the omniscience of a buddha, are primordially unestablished as any nature of dualistic phenomena—such as subject and object, cyclic existence and nirvana, self and other, or existence and non-existence. Even though they abide as the great, stainless, naturally pure equality of the single sphere of reality, which is primordially free from birth and cessation, when the adventitious delusion of not realizing this arises, then to the mind stained by the superimposition of self and phenomena, the object appears as impure, and because the mind grasps it as such, it is called an impure sentient being, possessing the stains and obscurations of the side of cyclic existence.

In order to remove those adventitious stains, the path of the three vehicles is taught. By entering that path, one sees the natural state of reality—that natural purity—ever more clearly. Through the manner of generating the realizations of the four fruits of the śrāvakas, the fruit of the pratyekabuddhas, and the nine stages of the bodhisattva’s path of seeing and path of meditation, one is said to have small, medium, or great purity in terms of abandoning the stains to be abandoned; these are called sentient beings who are purified to varying degrees of their stains.

Although there is no impurity from the beginning in the nature of objects such as form, because the adventitious stains of grasping in a distorted way are analogous to a sequence of purification—just as when an eye defect is cleared, one sees the object more clearly—the subject sees the purity of the object, and by virtue of seeing that, the subject is also called "purified." There is no other way of being purified that is separate from this. Thus, while in terms of the mode of appearance, it exists as if the subject is becoming purer and the object is also newly becoming pure, in terms of the mode of abiding, one should know that seeing the nature of objects such as form as primordially pure is itself the "fruit of primordial purity," which is the subject being freed from adventitious stains. Since these two are, from the beginning, of one meaning in the key point of abiding in the great purity where there is no duality of object and subject, one should know that these two purities are identical in essence.

Likewise, the purity of the fruit and the purity of form and so forth are the culmination of the purity of being free from adventitious stains; they become the purity of the primordial wisdom of omniscience, which has completely abandoned the two obscurations. All these purities have one key point in the meaning of the root, the natural purity, just as was explained.

Thus, these three—the purity of the culmination of omniscience, the purity of attaining the fruits of the various paths of the stages, and the purity of the phenomena of the basis, such as form, the aggregates, elements, and sense sources—are posited as distinct in terms of their mode of appearance. However, in terms of their mode of abiding, they are like the element of space, which has no distinctions; they are inseparable in the essence of the one naturally pure expanse of reality, and cannot be divided by the mind.

For the buddha’s primordial wisdom, which sees the natural state of that pure reality exactly as it is, all phenomena are seen as having the nature of being perfectly awakened or primordially beyond sorrow; there is no impurity. That primordial wisdom of realization is also the ultimate purity, having completely and permanently abandoned all obscurations, including the latent tendencies of adventitious stains. Therefore, knowing that all phenomena are of one taste, without distinction, as primordially pure and awakened—without the nature of dualistic phenomena such as object and subject, as they are seen by that wisdom—is the ultimate intent of the perfection of wisdom.

The manner of maintaining this in a state of "just resting" (cog bzhag) in the natural state is as follows:
There is nothing here to be removed,
And nothing here to be established.
Look perfectly at perfection itself;
When perfection is seen, one is completely liberated.
One should understand it in accordance with this.
